episode.title: Align approval and patch-safety decisions with the effective split filesystem policy
episode.before: At parent c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99, several core approval consumers still classified filesystem restriction through the legacy SandboxPolicy projection. Unmatched-command fallback and default execution approval derived allow/prompt behavior from legacy categories; shell, unified-exec, and intercepted-exec requests did not consistently supply the split filesystem policy to that decision boundary. Patch write safety also locally reconstructed readable and writable-root semantics instead of using the shared effective-access query. This allowed approval and patch-safety logic to diverge from the split policy carrying the actual filesystem carveouts.
episode.after: At c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9, execution approval decisions consume FileSystemSandboxPolicy directly: restricted access requires or permits escalation prompts as appropriate, while unrestricted or externally sandboxed access follows the non-restricted path. The effective policy is threaded through shell, unified-exec, orchestration, and intercepted-exec call sites. Patch write eligibility delegates to the shared can_write_path_with_cwd query. Regression tests establish that legacy sandbox_mode configurations construct equivalent split filesystem/network policies and round-trip without semantic drift, and that a restricted split policy controls escalation even when the legacy projection says danger-full-access.
episode.diff: The commit modifies nine core files (259 insertions, 76 deletions). It adds FileSystemSandboxPolicy to ExecApprovalRequest and intercepted-exec context, changes unmatched fallback and default approval classification to FileSystemSandboxKind, updates shell/orchestrator/unified-exec callers to pass the effective split policy, replaces manual patch-path calculations with can_write_path_with_cwd, and adds or updates regression tests for legacy-policy conversion, restricted approval behavior, and split-policy-driven unmatched-command escalation.

evidence_units.claim: Commit c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9 has parent c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99 and describes the change as aligning remaining core approval and patch-safety consumers with split filesystem-policy semantics, while explicitly excluding new platform backend enforcement.

Before the change, unmatched-command fallback matched legacy SandboxPolicy categories; afterward, OnRequest and Reject behavior matches FileSystemSandboxPolicy.kind, treating Restricted separately from Unrestricted and ExternalSandbox.
evidence_units.source: git diff c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99 c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9 -- codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs; post-change lines 493-563

evidence_units.claim: ExecApprovalRequest now carries both the compatibility sandbox policy and the effective filesystem sandbox policy, and ExecPolicyManager passes the latter into unmatched-command rendering.
The ordinary shell handler populates execution approval requests with the turn's file_system_sandbox_policy.
The unified-exec process manager supplies context.turn.file_system_sandbox_policy when evaluating an execution approval request.
Intercepted Unix execution packages the effective filesystem policy in InterceptedExecPolicyContext and passes it to the same unmatched-command decision function used by ordinary execution.
The default execution approval requirement now keys OnRequest and Reject behavior off FileSystemSandboxKind::Restricted instead of legacy SandboxPolicy variants.
Tool orchestration uses turn_ctx.file_system_sandbox_policy for both the initial default approval requirement and the later approval-state check.

Patch write-path safety no longer reconstructs unreadable and writable roots locally; it normalizes each path and delegates effective authorization to file_system_sandbox_policy.can_write_path_with_cwd.
evidence_units.source: git diff c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99 c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9 -- codex-rs/core/src/safety.rs; post-change lines 143-173

evidence_units.claim: A regression test supplies a restricted split filesystem policy alongside legacy DangerFullAccess and asserts that an unmatched escalation request produces Decision::Prompt, proving the split policy controls this decision.

Sandboxing tests assert that restricted filesystem access requires approval under OnRequest, external sandbox access skips it, and Reject configuration preserves its prompt-versus-auto-reject behavior.

A loader-level regression test covers danger-full-access, read-only, and workspace-write legacy configurations, asserting equivalent split filesystem and network policies and successful conversion back to the original legacy policy.

Intercepted-execution tests were updated to provide explicit restricted or unrestricted filesystem policies through InterceptedExecPolicyContext, exercising the new policy input across wrapper parsing and policy matching paths.

The commit records targeted validation commands for the no-drift loader test, request-permissions and intercepted-exec suites, restricted approval behavior, split-policy unmatched escalation behavior, explicit-policy tests, and codex-core clippy; the evidence bundle contains no status-check results, so execution success is not independently established here.

candidate_atomics.name: classify-approval-from-effective-filesystem-policy
candidate_atomics.title: Classify execution approval from effective filesystem access
candidate_atomics.description: Make default and unmatched-command approval outcomes depend on the effective split filesystem restriction kind rather than a lossy compatibility projection.

semantic_action.intent: Prevent execution approval prompts, skips, or rejections from disagreeing with the filesystem restrictions that will actually govern the command.
semantic_action.pre_state: Approval logic receives an approval mode and sandbox override request, but derives filesystem restriction from legacy sandbox categories that may disagree with the effective split policy.
semantic_action.post_state: Approval logic uses the effective filesystem policy kind: restricted access follows restricted approval and escalation behavior, while unrestricted or external access follows the non-restricted path.
semantic_action.validation: Exercise contradictory legacy/effective inputs and approval modes; verify restricted split access prompts for requested escalation, restricted OnRequest requires approval, external access skips default approval, and Reject settings retain configured auto-rejection behavior.

candidate_atomics.name: propagate-effective-filesystem-policy-to-execution-paths
candidate_atomics.title: Propagate effective filesystem policy through every execution path
candidate_atomics.description: Carry the same effective filesystem policy into ordinary shell, unified execution, tool orchestration, and intercepted execution so all paths invoke approval logic with the authoritative state.

semantic_action.intent: Eliminate execution paths that silently fall back to legacy filesystem semantics because the effective policy is absent at the approval boundary.
semantic_action.module_role: execution request and escalation context plumbing
semantic_action.pre_state: The turn owns an effective split filesystem policy, but one or more approval request structures or execution call sites do not carry it to the decision engine.
semantic_action.post_state: Every covered ordinary, persistent, orchestrated, and intercepted execution path supplies the turn's effective filesystem policy to approval classification.
semantic_action.validation: Compile and exercise shell-wrapper parsing, intercepted policy matching, ordinary shell approval, orchestration, and unified-exec request construction with the new required policy field.

candidate_atomics.name: delegate-patch-authorization-to-effective-access-query
candidate_atomics.title: Delegate patch authorization to the shared effective-access query
candidate_atomics.description: Replace locally reconstructed root and carveout checks with the filesystem policy's canonical path-write predicate.

semantic_action.intent: Keep patch safety consistent with the same precedence and carveout semantics used by the effective filesystem policy.
semantic_action.pre_state: Patch authorization separately computes unreadable roots, full-disk access, and writable-root membership, creating a duplicate interpretation of policy semantics.
semantic_action.post_state: Each normalized patch target is authorized by the shared effective filesystem write-access query using the current working directory.
semantic_action.validation: Run patch-safety tests over writable, non-writable, unreadable, and unrestricted targets and require their outcomes to match the effective policy query.

candidate_atomics.name: verify-legacy-policy-conversion-without-semantic-drift
candidate_atomics.title: Verify legacy configuration converts without permission drift
candidate_atomics.description: Establish a compatibility oracle that legacy sandbox modes produce equivalent split policies and can be reconstructed without changing their meaning.

semantic_action.intent: Preserve existing configuration behavior while consumers migrate to split filesystem and network policies.
semantic_action.pre_state: Legacy sandbox_mode inputs remain supported, but their conversion into split filesystem and network policies lacks regression coverage for semantic equivalence and round-trip reconstruction.
semantic_action.post_state: Representative unrestricted, read-only, and workspace-write legacy inputs are proven by assertions to construct the expected split policies and round-trip to the original legacy policy.
semantic_action.validation: Load each representative legacy configuration, compare generated filesystem and network policies with canonical conversions, then convert them back and assert equality with the original legacy policy.

candidate_workflows.name: align-permission-consumers-with-effective-filesystem-policy
candidate_workflows.title: Align permission decisions with effective filesystem access
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order resolution chain for migrating approval and write-safety consumers from a legacy permission projection to the authoritative split filesystem policy without changing compatibility behavior or platform enforcement.

workflow_graph.goal: Ensure every covered approval and patch-write decision reflects the effective filesystem restrictions and carveouts while preserving legacy configuration semantics.
when_to_use: A system has introduced a richer or split filesystem permission model but approval or safety consumers still inspect a legacy projection.
Different execution paths can reach the same approval decision with inconsistent policy inputs.
Local authorization code duplicates effective-access precedence or carveout calculations.
anti_goals: Do not introduce or redesign platform sandbox backend enforcement.
Do not change network-policy behavior except to verify legacy conversion equivalence.
Do not remove the legacy compatibility policy while call sites still require it for unrelated behavior.
Do not broaden filesystem access or suppress prompts merely to simplify the migration.
not_applicable_when: The effective filesystem policy is not available at runtime or has no authoritative access semantics.
The reported defect is solely in operating-system sandbox enforcement rather than approval or authorization consumers.
No before/after implementation and behavioral oracle can establish divergence from a legacy projection.
inputs: legacy compatibility policy and configuration inputs
all ordinary, unified, orchestrated, and intercepted execution entry points
patch target paths and working directory
targeted approval, configuration, interception, and patch-safety tests
workflow_graph.entry_state: An effective split filesystem policy exists, but remaining permission consumers or call paths can reconstruct decisions from a legacy projection or duplicated root logic.
workflow_graph.exit_state: Covered execution paths deliver the authoritative filesystem policy to approval logic; restricted, unrestricted, and external states produce policy-consistent decisions; patch writes use the shared effective-access predicate; and legacy configurations retain equivalent split and round-trip semantics.

steps.condition: Legacy permission configuration remains a supported input.
steps.validation: Representative legacy modes generate canonical split filesystem/network policies and round-trip to the original legacy policy.

steps.condition: Execution approval can be reached through multiple request or interception paths.
steps.validation: All covered request structures and call sites compile with and supply the effective filesystem policy; intercepted-execution tests exercise the context.

steps.condition: Approval behavior depends on whether effective filesystem access is restricted.
steps.validation: A deliberately contradictory legacy DangerFullAccess plus restricted split policy prompts for escalation, and default approval tests distinguish restricted from external access.

steps.condition: A patch or write-safety guard independently interprets roots, exclusions, or full-disk access.
steps.validation: The guard normalizes targets and obtains its decision from the canonical effective path-write predicate; targeted patch-safety tests must remain green.

validation_ladder: Compile the affected request and context structures so every approval path must provide an effective filesystem policy.
Run focused unit tests for restricted versus external default approval requirements and Reject-mode behavior.
Run the contradictory-policy unmatched-command test to prove the split policy, not the legacy projection, controls escalation prompting.
Run intercepted-execution tests to cover wrapper parsing and policy fallback with the propagated context.
Run legacy configuration conversion and round-trip regression tests across unrestricted, read-only, and workspace-write cases.
Run existing patch-safety tests against writable, denied, unreadable, and unrestricted targets.
Run the broader codex-core test suite and test-target clippy after focused tests pass.
stop_conditions: Stop if no authoritative effective filesystem policy can be identified.
Stop if a consumer requires semantics not represented by the effective policy; extend the policy contract before replacing its logic.
Stop and defer platform-specific enforcement failures to the backend work responsible for that platform.
Do not declare validation complete if only test source or commit-listed commands are available without execution results.
unresolved_or_deferred: The evidence bundle omits status checks and the extraction did not independently establish that the commit-listed test and clippy commands passed.
Linux backend parity, Windows fail-closed behavior, and shared precedence/model changes are explicitly assigned to adjacent changes rather than this episode.
The patch-safety implementation change is direct, but this commit adds no new dedicated patch-safety regression test; its oracle depends on the existing targeted test suite.

unresolved_questions: Did all commit-listed cargo test and clippy commands pass at the pinned implementation ref? The local bundle contains no status-check or execution-result evidence.

Which existing patch-safety tests most directly exercise unreadable-root carveouts after delegation to can_write_path_with_cwd? The implementation diff establishes the delegation, but no new dedicated test was added in this commit.
